A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RESCUE by the same authors. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated method-details and experimental appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, summarization-model experiments, and code-length and runtime analyses in Section 3 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds CWEval evaluations, cross-language tests, performance breakdowns, and fusion and threshold experiments in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The knowledge construction, program slicing, hierarchical retrieval, modified RRF, and generation procedures are retained. Algorithms 1-2 and the prompt templates are unchanged. Added explanations of CWE-level API aggregation and indexed vulnerability causes clarify the existing method.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original benchmarks and adds CWEval security tasks in Python and C/C++, followed by Go and JavaScript evaluations using languages absent from the knowledge base (Appendices C.4 and C.5.3). This substantially broadens security-task and language coverage.

E2.justification: The five main baselines remain SecCoder, Codexity, INDICT, SafeCoder, and CoSec. Table 12 adds standard RRF as an evaluated fusion comparator. The new CWEval comparisons reuse existing zero-shot and SecCoder comparators.

E3.justification: The added CWEval evaluation uses manually crafted dynamic functional and security tests with adversarial inputs, supplementing the original CodeQL-based security evaluation. Appendix C.6 also introduces a 20-task random validation subset with one threshold varied while the other two are fixed. Existing main-experiment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct performance analyses for seen versus unseen CWE types, cross-language transfer, and functionality-specific versus memory-related vulnerabilities. It also adds modified-versus-standard RRF ablation and sensitivity studies for all three retrieval thresholds. These extend the retained construction, hierarchy, facet, and summarizer analyses substantially.

E5.justification: The original 100- and 10-sample generation counts remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals, run-to-run variability, or significance tests; the new tables likewise provide point estimates and differences. Randomly selecting 20 validation tasks changes evaluation sampling, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained results are unchanged, including the CWE coverage table renumbered from Table 8 to Table 9. New Tables 8 and 10-16 add substantial benchmark, generalization, and sensitivity findings. For example, new CWEval results report Qwen2.5-Coder-7B SecurePass@1 of 43.70 for RESCUE, versus 36.80 for zero-shot and 36.00 for SecCoder.

T1.justification: The modified RRF and SecurePass@k definitions, clustering recursion, PDG reachability formulation, and Algorithms 1-2 are unchanged. The mathematical method details move from Appendix C to Appendix B without new proofs or substantive formal revisions.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same knowledge-construction and retrieval contributions. The headline 4.8-point SecurePass@1 improvement and the introduction's 98.7% functionality-retention claim remain unchanged. Additional evaluations support the existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 expands the earlier coverage-based generalization discussion with proposed explanations involving shared vulnerability patterns, transferable guidelines, and pretrained knowledge. It explains differences between vulnerability categories and adds explicit limitations concerning static-analysis errors and function-level applicability (Appendices C.5, C.7, and F). The existing overhead discussion is also expanded.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation repository link and reproducibility statement, and explicitly documents CWE-level API-set aggregation and the source of indexed vulnerability causes. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, preprocessing, algorithms, and prompt templates are retained; these additions primarily improve documentation and access information.

R1.justification: v2 adds five cited works: secure-generation research by Tony, Lin, and Xu and colleagues, CWEval by Peng and colleagues, and the vulnerability classification work by Chen and colleagues. The overall positioning against prior retrieval, fine-tuning, and tool-based approaches remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with local wording and explanatory refinements. v2 swaps the method-details and experimental appendices, expands Section 3.5's roadmap, and adds acknowledgment, ethics, reproducibility, limitations, and LLM-use sections.

P2.justification: New Tables 8 and 10-16 substantially expand the presentation with benchmark comparisons, language and vulnerability breakdowns, and threshold sweeps featuring colored gains and losses. Figure 1's task-analysis panel is revised, and tables and appendix material are relocated. Existing main result displays and Figure 3 retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: dynamic CWEval tests supplement v1's static security checks, while measured unseen-CWE and cross-language results address the earlier reliance on coverage counts for generalization. Fusion controls, explicit applicability limits, and code-access information further improve assessability. The threshold-robustness claim is overly broad given Llama's declines in Tables 14-15, but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
